defense_evidence_text: A nine-way internal comparison: three embedding models (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, GTE-large, MiniLM-L6-v2) crossed with three classifiers (XGBoost, LightGBM, Random Forest), with the OpenAI+XGBoost configuration best at 97.7% accuracy / 0.977 F1. Performance is described as matching or exceeding existing IPIA detection methods, but those methods are characterized from the literature rather than reimplemented and run on this dataset, so the cross-method comparison is indirect. The best configuration - OpenAI text-embedding-3-small embeddings with an XGBoost classifier - achieves 97.7% accuracy and an F1 of 0.977, which the authors report as matching or exceeding existing IPIA detection methods. The more practically consequential figure is inference cost: an average of 0.001 ms per sample, several orders of magnitude cheaper than LLM-based detection, which is what makes an always-on inline detection layer feasible rather than a design aspiration. Combined with model-agnosticism, this positions the method as a complement to prevention mechanisms rather than a replacement - it can be dropped into an existing pipeline without architectural change. The comparative design across three embedding models and three classifiers means the result identifies which component carries the performance rather than reporting a single tuned pipeline, though the strongest configuration depends on a proprietary API embedding model, which reintroduces an external dependency the rest of the design avoids. Proposes an embedding-based detector for Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks that works by analysing the semantic relationship between the user's stated intent and the external content retrieved into context, rather than by inspecting the external content in isolation. That relational framing is the paper's core idea: an injected instruction is anomalous not because of its own surface features but because it is semantically unrelated to what the user asked for, which is a signal a content-only filter cannot see. defense_evidence_text: No implemented head-to-head baseline. Comparison is argumentative, against two classes of prior approach characterized from the literature: static/rule-based heuristic filters (criticized for evaluating prompts without context, hence high false positive and false negative rates) and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation (credited with better contextual understanding but charged with 2-3 seconds of added latency per API call). Neither is re-implemented and measured on the same test set as Analy8. On an unseen test subset the classifier reports 92.46% overall detection accuracy with 100.00% precision for the malicious class - zero false positives, meaning every payload it flagged was genuinely adversarial, which the authors emphasize as the property that keeps legitimately complex benign queries from being blocked. The corresponding recall is 80.52%, so roughly one in five injection attempts is missed, and the F1 balances these at a substantially lower level than the headline accuracy suggests. This precision/recall asymmetry is the paper's real finding and it cuts both ways: as a deployed guardrail the layer is unusually safe against over-blocking, but as a security control it lets a fifth of attacks through to the execution engine, which for indirect prompt injection - where a single success can trigger an irreversible tool action - is a material gap the paper does not dwell on. The performance claim relative to LLM-as-a-judge rests on the architectural argument (a TF-IDF plus Random Forest pipeline avoids the cited 2-3 second per-call penalty) rather than on head-to-head latency measurements reported against an LLM judge baseline. The paper additionally positions itself against prior defenses characterized as addressing isolated pipeline stages without end-to-end integrity guarantees, but those are discussed rather than reimplemented and measured. The most interesting result is a metric artifact the paper confronts head-on. RAG-H's defended pipeline abstains - when retrieved documents do not provide sufficiently strong or consistent evidence, it refuses to answer or escalates for analyst review - and those refusals are scored as incorrect under the accuracy metric even though they are the safer behaviour. Consequently, on the poisoned corpus accuracy falls for both systems but the defended pipeline drops MORE sharply than the undefended baseline, precisely because it withholds judgment where the baseline keeps answering from adversarial context. Beyond this, the reported finding is directional rather than tabulated in the text available: layered trust, consistency and governance controls significantly mitigate poisoning effects and reduce Poison Impact Rate without unacceptable latency. This abstention-versus-wrong-answer distinction is the same structural point RQ6's Stage 3 test surfaced from the other direction - that whether a defense converts an attack into a refusal or into a wrong answer changes what accuracy metrics report - and it is a caution for reading any accuracy-only evaluation of a RAG defense in this corpus.
